KEY MESSAGE 1...Offshore storm brings continued enhanced
northerly gusts through Friday morning. Mainly light rain or
even light sprinkles are expected overnight tonight into early
on Thursday for the immediate southeast New England coastal
areas before tapering off Thursday afternoon.

There has been no substantial change to the forecast, messaging
and impacts to Southern New England through Friday regarding 
the distant offshore low pressure, now Subtropical Storm
Josephine, slowly meandering northward, located well to the east 
of the mouth of the Chesapeake Bay as of Wednesday afternoon.
This system is mainly bringing some lower-level cloud cover to
southeast New England, along with enhanced NE winds with gusts
in the 20-25 mph range over most of the mainland, and around
35-45 mph gusts for Cape Cod and the Islands. A rather sharp
gradient in cloud cover is noted north and west of I-95, being
governed by expansive surface ridging associated with a cooler 
and drier airmass. 

Composite radar mosaic imagery as of Wednesday afternoon is 
picking up on the western extent of the offshore system's rain 
shield in our far southeastern ocean waters; latest guidance 
continues to indicate a continued northwestward creep of this 
rain shield into the waters near the Islands and eventually 
spreading toward the south coast and Cape Cod tonight. This rain
shield will be fighting dry advection (e.g. dewpoints in the 
30s) as it attempts to progress north/west; even across the 
south coat and the Cape, rain intensities end up being quite 
light and could struggle to even measure/reach the ground. The 
best chance at steadiest light rains is across Nantucket and 
Martha's Vineyard overnight tonight into early Thursday morning.
As the distant offshore storm passes toward the northeast on 
Thursday, expect a decrease in both southeastern New England 
rain showers and a decrease in cloud cover. Dry weather is 
anticipated for the remainder of Thursday into Friday as 
reinforcing surface ridging builds back in from northern Canada.

The main impact for most of Southern New England ends up being 
enhanced northeast to northerly breezes, strongest for the Cape 
and Islands in the 35-45 mph range into Thursday noontime, 
before slowly decreasing into the 20-35 mph range Thursday night
into Friday. Seas will continue to build and remain rough, with
the greatest impact being for our marine interests. 

As has been the case the past couple days, differences in cloud
cover and northerly onshore winds has driven a wide range in 
temperatures. As the coastal low departs, it draws down an 
increasingly cool airmass in for Thursday night. Clear skies and
lighter northerly winds are supporting a larger diurnal range 
in temperatures across most areas along and northwest of I-95, 
with chilly nights and milder days with more sunshine. Lows 
tonight should range in the upper 30s to mid 40s from NW MA to 
I-95 and in between, with highs in the low to mid 60s on 
Thursday; with a cold airmass coming in Thursday night, lows are
in the 28-34F range for these same areas. Meanwhile toward the 
southeast coastal areas, a tighter diurnal range in temperatures
where cloud cover and northerly winds are the strongest. For 
these locations, high temperatures end up cooler in the mid to 
upper 50s are more common, while lows are "milder", in the mid 
40s to lower 50s due to the cloud cover and the breezes. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...Prolonged stretch of dry weather Friday into
Wednesday. Cooler Friday, followed by moderating temperatures
into Monday. Turning cooler toward the middle of next week.

Not much change to this portion of the forecast. High pressure 
dominates our weather into early next week, providing dry
weather. Turning cooler Friday with the initial arrival of this 
high pressure from eastern Canada, followed by moderating
temperatures into Monday.

The forecast for Tuesday and Wednesday gets more complex. A
front gets sandwiched between the initially discussed high
pressure, over the central Appalachians by Monday, and another
high pressure over Manitoba and Saskatchewan. This pattern makes 
it difficult to project the timing and movement of this front, 
as it will greatly depend on which high pressure is stronger. At
this time, thinking the high pressure over Canada will 
ultimately become the stronger of the two, with the result being
this front sweeping across southern New England some time 
Monday night into into Wednesday. Just how fast this happens, 
and how far south this front gets pushed, will need to be 
refined with later forecasts.

There does not appear to be much moisture associated with this 
front. At this time, the most likely outcome will just be a 
period clouds and lower temperatures mid week. That said, it 
would not take much additional moisture to warrant a mention of 
showers in later forecasts.
